sections.title: Robots on a Small Scale: Microrobotics

scenes.title: Human or Robot?
scenes.brief: A zoomable "frontier map" with three size bands (meter, millimeter, micrometer) holding robot emoji that open the other chapter-9 scenes. Center stage: a slate pole-balancing task with an orange joystick for the learner (human 🧑) or an autonomous loop (🤖). An orange slider adds round-trip delay; the pink cart response lags, a coral overshoot trace grows, and a phase-lag dial shows the loop going unstable past a threshold. A purple haptic-feedback arrow on the joystick shows force reflected back (telepresence).

scenes.title: Danger Zones
scenes.brief: A carousel of slate worlds: orbit (long arm on a shuttle bay), seabed (tethered vehicle with a hydraulic arm), reactor/mine (arm on a tracked cart behind a lead wall), burning building (legged bot on stairs), orchard (hand picking gold oranges). Each world has a coral "human risk" meter and a "signal delay" clock; dragging the world farther from Earth or deeper under water raises the delay until the orange joystick greys out and the robot must plan on its own (blue planned path).

scenes.title: Keyhole Hands
scenes.brief: Cutaway of a body wall (slate) with a small hole. A straight orange tool passes through the hole; the hole is a fixed pivot so the tool can only slide, twist, and tilt two ways (4 lime arrows; 2 coral crossed-out arrows for the missing tip orientations). The tip-orientation sphere shows only a thin reachable band. A shaky-hand slider adds purple tremor that the fulcrum filters only in the pivot directions. Toggle "add a wrist/fingers": a tiny multifingered pink hand at the tip restores full 6 lime arrows and the orientation sphere fills in.

scenes.title: Tiny Robots
scenes.brief: A size slider (meter → micron) shrinks a robot gripper. Bars for weight (∝ L³), electrostatic pull (∝ L²) and sticky surface forces (∝ L) re-rank as the size shrinks: gravity bar collapses, electrostatic bar wins. Next, a teal chip with blue square platforms floating on purple air jets, pushed by orange electrode pulses; drag a gold target and platforms glide. Last, a flat pink cut-out folds along hinges like origami into a 3D gripper when the water bath is shaken.

pages.summary: The closing chapter surveys where robotics is heading and frames teleoperation as the natural first step toward autonomy.

atoms.idea: Chapter 9 title: an outlook on future uses of robots.

The book chose compact mathematics, which hides the excitement: robots are already standard in car welding/painting and electronics assembly, while many other fields are only starting; the chapter surveys those.
atoms.feynman: Like a chef who taught you knife skills from a textbook and now walks you to the window to show the whole restaurant street you could open a shop on.
atoms.visual: Frontier map: three horizontal bands (meter, millimeter, micrometer). Lime filled robot icons in the "factory" corner (welding sparks, spray paint); hollow orange icons scattered elsewhere pulse as "still growing". Tapping an icon zooms into its scene.

atoms.idea: Teleoperation and robotics use the same hardware; they differ in whether a human or the machine closes the decision loop. New devices usually appear teleoperated first, but there are reasons to remove the human from the loop.
atoms.feynman: A remote-control toy car vs. a robot vacuum: same wheels and motors, but in one your thumb decides every turn.
atoms.visual: Pole-balancing cart: a toggle swaps the brain icon above the loop arrow between 🧑 and 🤖. Same orange motor arrows, same pink cart; only the loop arrow's source changes.

atoms.idea: Two reasons against a human in the loop: transmission delays for sensing and commanding, and slow human reaction to numerical data.
atoms.feynman: Steering a car by phone with a friend who describes the road three seconds late: you crash on every curve.
atoms.visual: Delay slider (orange) on the round-trip link; the pink cart response trails a ghost of the ideal; a coral wobble trace grows and the pole falls once delay passes a marked threshold. A second slider slows the "human reaction" stopwatch.

atoms.idea: Page 395

pages.summary: Teleoperators are treated as tomorrow's autonomous robots; telepresence ties to virtual reality; the survey is ordered by robot size, starting with hazardous environments and space.

atoms.idea: The authors treat today's teleoperated machines and tomorrow's autonomous ones as one family.
atoms.feynman: A bike with training wheels is still the same bike you will ride alone later.
atoms.visual: In the human/robot toggle, a slow fade lets the 🧑 hand gradually lift off the joystick as the 🤖 loop takes over a growing fraction (orange bar).

atoms.idea: Virtual reality synthesizes sights, sounds, touch and force; vision and sound are easy to deliver remotely, touch and force are hard. Remote manipulation (telepresence) needs all of them, so most VR work is really telepresence.
atoms.feynman: Video-calling a friend lets you see and hear their cat, but you can't feel it purr; to pet it remotely you'd need the fur to push back on your hand.
atoms.visual: Joystick with a purple force-feedback arrow: when the remote pink gripper presses a teal object, the purple arrow pushes back on the orange stick; toggling haptics off makes the gripper crush the object (coral flash).

atoms.idea: Progress will span teleoperation, virtual reality and dextrous manipulation; the chapter is organized by robot scale: conventional, millimeter, and micro/nano.
atoms.feynman: Like a set of nesting dolls: big robot, little robot, tiny robot, each opened in turn.
atoms.visual: The frontier map's zoom slider snaps through three scale bands (1 m, 1 mm, 1 µm), each lighting up its scene icon.

atoms.idea: Section 9.1: robots in hazardous environments.
Conventional-size robots are most promising where people are at risk.
atoms.feynman: Send the toy truck, not your hand, into the hot oven.
atoms.visual: Danger-zone carousel opens; each world shows a coral human-risk meter beside a robot icon.

atoms.idea: Subheading: space.

Space examples: a long six-joint arm on the shuttle, normally teleoperated by sight but able to move in Cartesian mode under computer control; planned two-arm satellite servicers; planetary rovers with sampling arms that must act alone because signal delay is too long.
atoms.feynman: Playing catch with someone on the Moon: by the time your "now!" arrives, the ball has already landed.
atoms.visual: Orbit world: a long 6-joint arm (orange joints) on a shuttle bay grabs a gold satellite. Drag the world from orbit to Mars: the delay clock grows from 0 s to minutes, the joystick greys out, and the rover's blue planned path to a gold rock appears instead.

atoms.idea: Page 396

pages.summary: Hazardous-environment robots underwater, in nuclear/toxic/mining work, and in firefighting, construction, agriculture and meat processing.

atoms.idea: Subheading: underwater.

Remotely operated underwater vehicles inspect rigs and explore, replacing costly, risky divers; they are tethered or free platforms with arms, usually hydraulic for strength and corrosion; fully autonomous ones will grow where human reaction is too slow.
atoms.feynman: A puppet on a long string dangled into a deep well: the deeper it goes, the more you wish it could think for itself.
atoms.visual: Seabed world: a blue vehicle on a slate umbilical with a hydraulic arm (thick orange joints). Cut-tether toggle: the vehicle must explore by itself, revealing a teal occupancy map of the seafloor.

atoms.idea: Subheading: nuclear, toxic waste and mining.
Robotics grew partly out of manipulators for radioactive material; mobile robots with arms now inspect, maintain and handle spent fuel; toxic-waste and mining robots will spread.
atoms.feynman: The long tongs you use to grab a hot coal from a fire, grown into a whole machine.
atoms.visual: Reactor world: a master arm on the safe side of a slate lead wall mirrors its motion onto a slave arm on the coral hot side moving glowing rods; the coral dose meter stays at zero on the human side.

atoms.idea: Subheading: firefighting, construction, agriculture.

Fire robots could get building maps, sense heat/smoke, drag hoses and send video, needing legs as well as wheels for stairs; automated construction is young; vision-guided multifingered hands have picked fruit and harvested crops.
atoms.feynman: A firefighter dog that already knows the floor plan and carries the hose up the stairs.
atoms.visual: Fire world: a legged robot follows a gold path up slate stairs where a wheeled one stalls (coral 🚫). Orchard world: a pink multifingered hand closes on a gold orange; a teal camera cone finds it first.

atoms.idea: Robots have also been used for deboning meat and for shearing sheep, the latter needing a singularity-free wrist.
atoms.feynman: A barber who must follow the curves of a wiggly customer without ever getting their elbow locked.
atoms.visual: Wrist close-up: a standard 3-joint wrist sweeps its orientation sphere; at a coral pole it locks (manipulability ellipse flattens). Switch to the redesigned wrist: the coral pole is pushed outside the lime working zone.

atoms.idea: Page 397

pages.summary: Minimally invasive surgery is booming but is limited by tools that pivot at the incision and lack degrees of freedom.

atoms.idea: The shearing robot's wrist was designed to have no singularities inside the workspace [114].
atoms.feynman: A neck that can look anywhere you need without ever getting stuck staring straight up.
atoms.visual: Continuation of the wrist close-up: the lime workspace patch on the orientation sphere never touches the coral singular point.

atoms.idea: Section 9.2: medical applications for multifingered hands.

Minimally invasive surgery reaches organs through incisions of a few millimeters, cutting recovery time and risk; slender probes carry light, cameras and tools; modern imagers give clear internal views; scope types are matched to body cavities; such procedures, e.g. gall bladder removal, have become routine and may overtake open surgery.
atoms.feynman: Building a ship in a bottle: everything goes through the neck, and you watch through the glass.
atoms.visual: Cutaway: a slate body wall with three small ports; a teal camera cone lights a gold organ; orange tools slide in. A counter compares incision length (open vs. keyhole) with a shrinking coral recovery bar.

atoms.idea: The bottleneck is manipulator technology: passive tools transmit hand motion poorly and block touch; a tool pivoting in a port has only four freedoms (slide, twist, two tilts), so orientation is not fully controlled and stitches must radiate from the port.
atoms.feynman: A chopstick pushed through a hole in a cardboard box: you can poke, spin and tip it, but never bend its tip sideways inside.
atoms.visual: The tool pivots about the hole (fixed orange ring). Four lime arrows (slide, twist, tilt-x, tilt-y); two coral crossed arrows for missing tip yaw/pitch. Drawing a stitch line: only lines through the port's shadow turn lime.

atoms.idea: Page 398

pages.summary: Fine-motion and tremor limits motivate miniature multifingered surgical hands, teleoperated at first; then microrobotics is introduced.

atoms.idea: Second limit: fine control. Open surgeons brace against tremor; in keyhole surgery the fulcrum damps tremor in pivoting but not in other directions driven by shoulder and elbow shake.
atoms.feynman: Writing with a long pencil pushed through a hole: wiggles side-to-side get shrunk by the hole, but pushing in and out still shakes.
atoms.visual: Tremor slider adds purple jitter to the surgeon's hand. Tip trace: jitter is scaled down in the two tilt directions (lever ratio readout) but passes straight through along the slide axis.

atoms.idea: Many-DOF manipulators would help but are kinematically hard; tiny multifingered hands are proposed. At millimeter size, joints cannot be driven directly, so cables or micro-hydraulics are used, built with chip-fabrication methods; materials are strong enough, but actuators lack range of motion.
atoms.feynman: A marionette hand moved by strings because there is no room for motors inside the tiny fingers.
atoms.visual: Toggle "add fingers": a pink three-fingered hand unfolds at the tool tip; orange cables run back along the shaft; the orientation sphere fills from a thin band to full lime. A range-of-motion arc per joint shows small coral limits.

atoms.idea: Initially the surgeon would drive the hand by teleoperation: a sensor glove measures finger positions and feeds back touch and force [19].
atoms.feynman: A glove puppet in reverse: your fingers move and a tiny hand far away copies them and tells you what it feels.
atoms.visual: Glove on the left: orange finger joints. Mini hand on the right mirrors them; when it touches teal tissue, a purple pressure bubble appears on the matching glove fingertip.

atoms.idea: Remote surgery could serve battlefields and space; smarter, sensing manipulators point toward surgical workstations.
atoms.feynman: A doctor who can operate on a patient on the other side of the world, like a pilot flying a drone.
atoms.visual: Frontier map link: a dashed line from a surgeon console to a field tent and a space station; the delay clock appears again on the long link.

atoms.idea: Section 9.3: microrobotics.
Handling cells or chip parts needs scales orders of magnitude below surgical millirobots: micro and nano robots.
atoms.feynman: Lego for ants.
atoms.visual: Size slider sweeps from a hand (1 m) past a surgical gripper (1 mm) to a cell (10 µm); the robot shrinks alongside with a log-scale ruler.

atoms.idea: Page 399

pages.summary: Shrinking robots to part size brings gentler forces, accuracy and chip-style fabrication; micromachining and scaling of forces change actuation; an integrated chip of air-bearing platforms is described.

atoms.idea: Small objects can be handled by a huge precise arm or by a miniature robot; shrinking gives gentle forces, better accuracy and batch silicon fabrication.
atoms.feynman: Picking up a crumb with tweezers instead of a forklift.
atoms.visual: Split screen: a giant blue arm with a tiny pink tip vs. a micro gripper the size of the teal part. A "push force" bar for each: the micro one is naturally gentle.

atoms.idea: Robots on a chip were popularized by several groups [16, 91–93]; they envision micro-teleoperation in cramped spaces and massively parallel handling of tiny parts; challenges are summarized from [31].
atoms.feynman: An ant colony: many tiny workers each carrying one grain, all at once.
atoms.visual: A grid of dozens of identical micro grippers each grabs a teal grain simultaneously; a counter shows parts moved per second vs. a single big arm.

atoms.idea: Micro systems need power, propulsion, sensing-plus-control and communication; micromachining builds cilia arrays, tiny grippers, rotary motors and gyros; at small scale electrostatic forces dominate electromagnetic ones, so actuation must be rethought.
atoms.feynman: A dust speck sticks to your TV screen and ignores gravity: at its size, static cling beats weight.
atoms.visual: Scaling race: as the size slider shrinks L, bars for weight (∝L³), magnetic (∝L³–L⁴) and electrostatic (∝L²) forces re-rank live; a crossover point flashes when electrostatic becomes the tallest bar.

atoms.idea: An integrated planar manipulation chip [92]: a 1 cm² silicon bed with an air bearing floats 1 mm² platforms driven electrostatically, carrying grippers/probes/tools, with capacitive position sensing; modeled on a macro planar robot system and aimed at aligning and splicing optical fibers (Fig 9.1).
atoms.feynman: Air-hockey pucks that are steered by invisible tugs from the table instead of by mallets.
atoms.visual: Teal chip with purple air jets; blue square platforms hover. Orange electrode strips pulse in sequence to tug a platform toward a dragged gold target; teal capacitive sensors read its position (number readout).

atoms.idea: Today's micro-mechanisms are mostly flat.
atoms.feynman: Like stickers: everything printed lies flat on the sheet.
atoms.visual: All parts on the chip lie in one plane; tilting the camera shows zero height.

atoms.idea: Page 400

pages.summary: Figure of floating probe platforms; micro-hinges let flat-fabricated parts fold up into 3D; outlook on explosive growth of microrobots.

atoms.label: Fig 9.1
atoms.idea: Figure: several probing platforms floating on a shared air-bearing surface, and a close-up of one platform with its probe, sensing circuitry, air holes and electrodes.
atoms.feynman: A tray of floating pucks, each with its own little feeler poking out.
atoms.visual: Exploded view of one blue platform: purple air holes below, orange electrodes at the edges, teal sensing patch, pink probe tip; zoom out to many platforms gliding on one bed.

atoms.idea: 3D micro-structures can be made by fabricating flat pieces with micro-hinges that rotate or slide into place; origami-inspired designs can self-assemble when agitated in water after fabrication [93].
atoms.feynman: A pop-up birthday card: printed flat, it stands up into a castle when you open it.
atoms.visual: A flat pink cut-out with orange hinge lines; a "shake" button jiggles the water bath and the panels rotate about their hinges into a 3D gripper (rotation angles counted up to 90°).

atoms.idea: Outlook: rapid growth of swimming micro-machined robots and tiny multifingered manipulators for biology and electronics.
atoms.feynman: Like seeds scattered across a field, a forest of tiny robots is about to sprout.
atoms.visual: Frontier map finale: the micrometer band fills with swimming robot icons and tiny hands, all pulsing lime.

atoms.idea: Page 401
